newsitem.title: GERMANY: German churches urge media, Internet controls.
newsitem.headline: German churches urge media, Internet controls.

text.p: Germany's Catholic and Protestant churches on Wednesday issued a joint warning against the concentration of media power in the hands of a few and called for greater controls on the Internet.

Church leaders called on business executives and politicians not to allow profit motives and technology alone to drive developments, criticising an increase in the portrayal of sex and violence on television and on computer networks.
"Existing forms of regulation and voluntary control must be expanded in light of the demands of new media technology," said Bishop Karl Lehmann, head of the German Catholic Bishops Conference.
"Especially in regard to the increasing instrumentalisation of violence and intimacy for the purposes of entertainment we must demand voluntary commitments from providers."
He added: "This is particularly true for Internet providers."

Germany is embroiled in a debate over how much regulatory control to impose on the Internet. Several police teams are combing computer networks to root out criminal activity ranging from illegal pornography to extremist writings.

Prosecutors in Munich earlier this month indicted the head of the German subsidiary of U.S. online service CompuServe Corp on allegations of aiding in the trafficking of pornography, neo-Nazi writings and games that glorify violence.
The indictment followed a year-long investigation into whether CompuServe allowed members to access computers on the Internet that contained pornography and neo-Nazi writings.

The government itself is split on the issue because it fears that too much regulation, or taking the wrong regulatory steps, could impede investment in information technology and services, expected to create many jobs in years to come.

Bishop Klaus Engelhardt, head of the Council of Protestant Churches in Germany, warned against a division of society into information "haves" and "have nots", and the concentration of media power at the expense of diversity and freedom of expression.
"We are all affected by these media developments," he said.
"They must not be determined alone by technology and the economy, but rather must be shaped politically."
